questions.q: Why does this lesson argue documenting the 'why' behind a decision matters more than documenting the 'what'?
options: Because the 'what' never matters at all
Because the 'what' is usually still inspectable later by opening the org, but the reasoning behind why one alternative was chosen over another is much harder to reconstruct without a written record
Because Salesforce automatically documents every 'what' in its own audit trail with full reasoning included
Because 'why' documentation is required by Salesforce's terms of service
questions.explain: The lesson's core point is that the built result is still visible later, but the reasoning behind why it was chosen over its alternatives is what gets lost without a deliberate record.

questions.q: What are the four parts of this lesson's lightweight decision-record format?
options: Objective, Scope, Budget, Timeline
Context, Decision, Alternatives considered, Consequences
Requirements, Design, Build, Test
Owner, Reviewer, Approver, Date
questions.explain: The lesson's ADR-style format covers Context (the prompting requirement/situation), Decision (what was decided), Alternatives considered (what else was on the table and why it wasn't chosen), and Consequences (what the decision commits the team to).

questions.q: Per this lesson, which of these choices is worth recording as a decision record?
options: Creating a field named Status__c to hold a status value
Choosing a custom object over the standard Asset object because Asset's fields didn't cover rental-specific tracking needs
Any field's help text wording
The exact pixel spacing of a Lightning page layout
questions.explain: The lesson distinguishes decisions with a real, plausible alternative someone might later question (custom object vs. standard Asset) from routine configuration choices that belong in ordinary technical documentation instead.

questions.q: Why does this lesson warn against treating every small configuration choice as decision-record-worthy?
options: Because doing so dilutes the log until nobody reads it anymore, defeating the purpose just as thoroughly as not keeping a decision log at all
Because Salesforce limits the number of decision records an org can store
Because small configuration choices are always technically incorrect
Because decision records can only be written by a Technical Architect
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly warns that over-recording routine choices dilutes the decision log's usefulness, which defeats the purpose of keeping one in the first place.

questions.q: How does a documented decision protect a design, per this lesson's closing argument?
options: It guarantees the design can never be changed again

It prevents a future developer from accidentally undoing a deliberate, correctly-reasoned trade-off out of good intentions, by making any later change to that decision a deliberate, informed choice rather than an accidental regression
It has no real protective effect on the design at all
It replaces the need for design review entirely
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly argues that a decision record doesn't freeze a design forever, but it does prevent a well-meaning future change from accidentally reversing a trade-off that was deliberate and may still be correct.
